In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate and transport of two antibiotic-resistance genes in runoff from agricultural fields receiving different types of soil amendment.
the effects of soil amendments and vegetative cover on the transport of antibiotic resistance genes in storm runoff from agricultural fields.
the transport of ARGs in runoff from agricultural fields amended with manures from antibiotic-treated dairy cattle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of antibiotic resistance genes in runoff is influenced by the type of soil amendment and the timing of storm events.

the use of manure-derived soil amendment (composted or raw manure) increases the potential for the transport of antibiotic resistance genes in storm runoff, particularly in early storms, but the use of compost from antibiotic-treated cattle is not significantly different from compost from antibiotic-free cattle.

manure-amended fields release higher quantities of two ARGs, and, in storm runoff relative to fertilizer-only plots, and that composted manure did not mitigate ARG transport in runoff relative to raw manure-amendment plots.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

manure-amended fields, particularly those amended with raw manure, are likely to release higher concentrations of antibiotic resistance genes in runoff than fields amended with compost or chemical fertilizer alone.
the use of manure-derived soil amendment in agriculture may pose an additional risk to the spread of ARGs via runoff.
composting does not reduce ARGs in runoff.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the presence and transport of ARGs in agricultural runoff should be considered as an important water quality issue, and that composted manure may be no better than raw manure at reducing ARG transport.
ARGs can be transported from land-applied manures in runoff and that this transport may occur in the absence of detectable FIB.
ARG transport in runoff is influenced by storm events and that the use of manure-derived soil amendment may contribute to increased ARG levels in runoff.
